Firefighter: ‘Miracle’ no deaths in burning jet at DIA

DENVER ” It was a miracle that no one was killed when an airliner veered sharply off a runway during takeoff, burst into flames and nearly broke apart, firefighters said Sunday.

There was no official word on the possible cause of the crash of Continental Flight 1404 at Denver International Airport, which injured 38 people. Cockpit and voice recorders were recovered and appeared to be in good condition, the National Transportation Safety Board said Sunday.

The entire right side of the Boeing 737-500 was burned in the Saturday evening accident, and melted plastic from overhead compartments dripped onto the seats. Investigators said the plane’s left engine was ripped away along with all the landing gear.

----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------

“It was a miracle … that everybody survived the impact and the fire,” said Bill Davis, an assistant Denver fire chief assigned to the airport. “It was just amazing.”

A crack encircled much of the fuselage near the trailing edge of the wings, Davis said.

----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------

Davis, one of the firefighters who rushed to the scene, said the plane came to a rest about 200 yards from one of the airport’s four fire stations. Passengers walked out of the ravine in 24-degree cold and crowded inside the station, he said.

The 110 passengers and five crew members left the plane on emergency slides, officials said.

Passenger Emily Pellegrini told The Denver Post that as the plane headed down the runway, “It was bumpy, then it was bumpier, then it wasn’t bumpy.”

Gabriel Trejos told KUSA-TV in Denver that the plane buckled toward its middle and that the seats felt like they were closing in on him, his pregnant wife and his 13-month-old son, who was on his lap. His knees were bruised from the seat in front of him.

Maria Trejos told KUSA that there was an explosion and that the right side of the plane, where they were sitting, became engulfed in flames. The family used an emergency exit and slid down the wing of the jet to the ground.

The injuries included broken bones, but Robert Sumwalt, an NTSB member, didn’t know whether they were caused by the impact or the evacuation. Two people were initially listed in critical condition at the University of Colorado Hospital in Denver but were upgraded Sunday, one to serious and one to fair, spokeswoman Tonya Ewers said.

Continental Airlines spokeswoman Julie King said fewer than seven people were still in the hospital Sunday morning.

The plane veered off course about 2,000 feet from the end of the runway and did not appear to have gotten airborne, city aviation manager Kim Day said.

Investigators said Sunday evening that work would start again at daybreak. Robert Sumwalt, an NTSB member, said the damaged plane would remain for several days in the 40-foot-deep ravine where it landed. That runway will remain closed during the investigation, he said.

The weather was cold but not snowy when the plane took off on a flight to Houston around 6:20 p.m. Saturday.

The ravine in which the plane came to rest sits between runways. Flat land is rare on the plains abutting the Rocky Mountains near Denver, and the airport was built on gently rolling country. The runways are elevated so rain and snow will drain away.

Jim Proulx, a Boeing spokesman, said the company was supporting the NTSB investigation and sending representatives to Denver on Sunday night. He declined to comment on whether Boeing had any indication of possible problems with the 737-500 jetliner.

Controller cool-headed in DIA crash – The Denver Post

Air-traffic controller Tom Hedeen kept his cool the night Continental Airlines flight 1404 crashed at DIA in December, calmly directing fire and rescue vehicles to the scene as he moved other aircraft out of the way.

With the permission of federal air-safety officials, the National Air Traffic Controllers Association today released an audiotape of Hedeen’s commands to airport and airline personnel on the evening of Dec. 20, after the Continental 737 exited the left side of runway 34 Right and bounced over rough terrain until it came to a stop in a ravine nearly one-half mile from the runway.

All 110 passengers and five crew members escaped the fractured jet as flames consumed the aircraft’s right side.

“Ops 9,” Hedeen told a DIA airfield operations employee, “just had an aircraft departure off 34 Right, exited the runway at Whiskey Charlie (taxiway WC), appears to be on fire immediately adjacent to the firehouse. Red alert.”

Airport-operations personnel control the movement of emergency vehicles on DIA’s runways and taxiways.

From his perch in the Federal Aviation Administration tower 300 feet above the C concourse, Hedeen helped correct confusion among emergency personnel during the first seconds of their response.

“Ops 9, traffic’s coming out of the (fire) station going the wrong way,” Hedeen said. “They need to go eastbound out of the firehouse.”

Seconds later, to another operations employee, Hedeen continued to calmly and precisely offer direction for emergency vehicles to the crash scene: “Ops 7, west of runway 34 Right, immediately north of Whiskey Charlie, immediately east of the fire house, on fire, in the ditch, off the runway.”

Still there was some confusion among rescuers.

“Ops 7, it appears your truck is going southbound on 34 Right,” Hedeen said. “Is that what they want to do, away from the aircraft?”

“I’ll turn ’em around tower,” Ops 7 responded.

Hedeen again to the operations employee: “Just north of Whiskey Charlie, you’ll see the glow coming out. I can see the flames right now.”

Ops 7: “I have it tower, I have it. I have the glow.”

On Tuesday in Las Vegas, Hedeen will be among 16 controllers honored for their efforts as part of the union’s annual Communicating for Safety conference.

Hedeen, a controller for 17 years, is being recognized for “his composure and his professionalism,” said tower controller Richard Foster, who was with Hedeen in the tower on Dec. 20. Foster is president of the union local in the DIA tower.

The controllers union said Hedeen was not available for interviews, but Foster, who replaced Hedeen at his position that night, said as the men watched the smoke and flames from the tower window: “We thought we were watching people die.”

Jeffrey Leib: 303-954-1645 or jleib@denverpost.com

brut.title: NTSB cites pilot error in 2008 crash at DIA – The Denver Post

webpage.text:
NTSB cites pilot error in 2008 crash at DIA – The Denver Post

The captain of the Continental Airlines jet that crashed at Denver International Airport in 2008 during takeoff in gusty crosswinds should have been able to keep the plane on the runway if he had continued to make proper rudder adjustments, according to air-safety investigators.

Wind gusts reached as high as 45 knots, or 51 mph, during the takeoff roll of Continental Flight 1404 on Dec. 20, 2008, the National Transportation Safety Board said.

The safety board said Capt. David Butler’s failure to make the proper right-rudder adjustment was a probable cause of the accident.

The rudder is a vertical flight-control device on the plane’s tail that pilots use to stay on the runway center line during takeoffs.

The NTSB said contributing factors to the accident included an air-traffic-control system failure to disseminate “key, available wind information to the air-traffic controllers and pilots” and “inadequate crosswind training in the airline industry due to deficient simulator wind-gust modeling.”

Greg Feith, a Denver-based aviation-safety consultant and former NTSB accident investigator, said it may be unfair to expect that Butler could have made the correct rudder adjustment and kept the plane on the runway after it was hit with the sudden, high-intensity wind gust during takeoff.

“Investigators have months to dissect a pilot’s performance,” Feith said. “That pilot had seconds or milliseconds to process the information and take corrective action.”

After the Boeing 737-500 exited runway 34 Right, it traveled over uneven terrain, losing an engine and its main landing gear, before coming to rest with the fuselage cracked in half and the right side of the plane on fire.

All 110 passengers and five crew members escaped, although six people were seriously injured, including Butler.

First Officer Chad Levang, Butler’s co-pilot, two flight attendants and 38 passengers suffered minor injuries, the NTSB said.

“The accident pilots’ injuries would have likely been lessened or eliminated if their seats had been designed to meet the crashworthiness requirements . . . to which other airplane seats are designed,” the agency said. One of the NTSB’s recommendations was to upgrade the crashworthiness of pilots’ seats.

Butler has resumed flying for Continental, said Julie King, a spokeswoman for the airline.

“Safety is Continental’s top priority. We respect the NTSB investigative process and will carefully review today’s findings.”

NTSB board chairwoman Deborah Hersman said the flight attendants on Flight 1404 — whose actions in assisting the evacuation of passengers from the damaged plane have been described as heroic — were “a shining example of the things that went right that evening.”

“This accident was nothing less than the holiday miracle,” she said, referring to the lack of fatalities.

Among the NTSB’s other conclusions from the crash investigation:

• There was no evidence of pre-accident failure of the plane’s engines, structures or systems.

• Butler’s use of the nosewheel steering tiller and full right control wheel in the three seconds before the plane veered off the runway “likely resulted from acute stress stemming from a sudden, unexpected threat, perceived lack of control, and extreme time pressure.”

• The captain’s call for an aborted takeoff was delayed about 2 to 4 seconds because he was occupied with the steering tiller and control wheel, “both of which were ineffective and inappropriate for steering the airplane.”

• Because Continental’s simulator training did not replicate gusting crosswinds and because it was unlikely that Butler had previously encountered wind conditions that arose the night of the accident, “the captain was not adequately prepared to respond. “

Butler, a former Navy pilot who joined Continental in 1997, has more than 13,000 total flight hours, nearly half in Boeing 737 jets.

The NTSB said that while an air-traffic controller had given Butler and Levang information just before takeoff that winds were “270 at 27” — that is from the west at 27 knots, or about 31 mph — the controller also had information from other sensors showing DIA winds as high as 35 knots, gusting to 40 knots.

“If the accident pilots had received the most adverse available wind information . . . the captain would likely have decided to delay the departure or request a different runway,” the NTSB said, because the winds exceeded Continental’s recommended crosswind limit of 33 knots for that type of plane.

“Given the wind-related information the pilots had, their decision to proceed with a takeoff on 34R as planned was reasonable,” the agency said.

Jeffrey Leib: 303-954-1645 or jleib@denverpost.com

Twitter ye not: crash survivor updates blog from burning plane | X

When a Continental Airlines Boeing 737 skidded off the runway at Denver airport on Saturday, the 155 passengers and crew might have been understandably preoccupied with how they would escape from a plane that was being engulfed by flames. But for software engineer Mike Wilson the first priority was to report on his disrupted travel arrangements to his followers on the blogging site Twitter.

Over the ensuing hours he delivered a detailed account of the crash and its aftermath to users of the service - down to the airline's failure to offer him a stiff drink. Here is a selection of entries from his Twitter feed.

14 December, 4.06pm Whew! Christmas shopping pretty much done. 100% online except for a couple of gift certs.

20 December, 5.25pm Holy fucking shit, I was just in a plane crash!

5.58pm This was crash No 2 for me. Maybe I should start taking the bus.

8.22pm You have your wits scared out of you, drag your butt out of a flaming ball of wreckage and you can't even get a vodka-tonic. Boo.

11.22pm [From computer at home] Sorry for the radio silence, but my battery died in the middle of all this and I just made it home.

11.57pm Pretty exhausted at this point, so I'm heading off to bed. Good night!

21 December, 8.29am Waiting in the continental club for the "replacement" flight. Noticing I'm a little sore.

5.25pm I'm sitting as close to the exit as possible this time.

7.57pm Touchdown! Crowd goes wild!
